overview: This two-page secret memorandum, received by the U.S. Department of State in late November or early December 1934 and attributed to Pan American Airways, reports a Japanese Communications Ministry program to expand civil aviation and air-mail services while coordinating them with army and naval aeronautics. The projected ¥100 million program combined pilot training, aircraft acquisition, airfields, radio stations, and meteorological facilities with an extensive network of domestic and imperial routes. Its first stage emphasized services within Japan and to Taiwan, Korea, and the South Seas Mandate; a more speculative second stage envisioned connections to Southeast Asia, Sakhalin, Kamchatka, and Alaska, partly in response to Soviet and American aviation.

subfiles.title: Memorandum on Japan’s civil aviation and air-mail expansion program
subfiles.to: U.S. Department of State, Division of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.about: Reports a two-stage Japanese program for expanding civil aviation infrastructure and air-mail routes in coordination with army and naval aviation.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum describes a projected ¥100 million Communications Ministry program encompassing civilian pilot training, improved flying facilities, additional aircraft, and integration with military aeronautics. The first stage proposed eight domestic and imperial air-mail services linking Japan with Taiwan, Korea, Palau, and numerous Japanese cities. A less definite second stage proposed seven further networks extending toward Southeast Asia, Sakhalin, Kamchatka, and across Japan; the Kamchatka proposal was explicitly characterized as a response to Soviet service and American aviation in Alaska.

interest: The memorandum is valuable evidence of how ostensibly civilian communications infrastructure was understood as part of Japan’s wider military and imperial aviation system in 1934. Its route lists map Japan’s metropolitan and colonial geography while also revealing ambitions to enter Southeast Asian and North Pacific networks. Particularly notable is the explicit strategic framing of the Kamchatka route as a countermeasure to Soviet air mail and American airlines in Alaska, as well as Pan American Airways’ apparent role in supplying aviation intelligence to the State Department.
